plan.question: Compare single-agent and multi-agent support automation for a 20-person SaaS company, considering complexity, cost, reliability and safeguards.

alternatives.name: Single-agent support automation
defining_features: One primary agent handles support requests end to end
May use tools or retrieval, but does not delegate to other autonomous agents

alternatives.name: Multi-agent support automation
defining_features: Multiple specialized agents or roles collaborate or hand off work
Requires coordination, routing, and shared context between agents
Enables task specialization but adds orchestration and inter-agent failure modes

criteria.description: Engineering and operational effort to build, integrate, monitor, and maintain the approach for a 20-person SaaS company.

anchors.poor: Requires substantial orchestration, specialized expertise, and ongoing maintenance beyond what a 20-person SaaS company can reasonably support.
anchors.plausible: Can be implemented and maintained with manageable effort, but requires meaningful integration or operational work.
anchors.strong: Straightforward to build, integrate, and maintain with limited engineering and operational overhead.

criteria.description: Expected total cost of implementation and ongoing operation, including model usage, infrastructure, tooling, and maintenance.

anchors.poor: Likely to create materially higher or difficult-to-predict costs for a small SaaS company, with little clear cost control.
anchors.plausible: Costs appear manageable but depend on usage, tooling, or ongoing maintenance and need active monitoring.
anchors.strong: Likely to remain economical at the company's scale, with costs that are relatively simple to estimate and control.

criteria.description: Ability to resolve support requests accurately and consistently, including handling failures, escalation, and end-to-end task completion.

anchors.poor: Coordination or execution failures are difficult to detect or recover from, and the approach offers weak consistency or escalation.
anchors.plausible: Can handle common requests consistently, but has notable failure cases or requires human review and recovery procedures.
anchors.strong: Provides dependable outcomes for the intended support workload, with clear failure detection, recovery, and human escalation.

criteria.description: Ability to enforce access controls, privacy and data boundaries, approval requirements, auditability, and safe escalation in customer support workflows.

anchors.poor: Difficult to constrain or audit actions and data access, with weak control over unsafe or unauthorized behavior.
anchors.plausible: Supports practical guardrails and human review, but controls or auditability require additional design and monitoring.
anchors.strong: Makes it straightforward to enforce least privilege, approval gates, data boundaries, audit trails, and escalation.

assumptions: Assume the comparison concerns architectures for automating customer support workflows, not specific vendors or products.
Assume the company has a modest engineering and operations capacity typical of a 20-person SaaS company.
Assume the support workload, ticket volume, existing systems, and regulatory obligations are unspecified; assess trade-offs generally rather than against a particular deployment.
No stated priority for implementation_complexity, total_cost, reliability, safeguards: equal default weight 3.
